Here the dossier says "travel documents and any local identity check will continue to show the sex assigned at birth" — this is about local residents' documents. A visitor's passport is from home country; if their home passport matches their gender, no issue. But if the visitor's passport shows birth sex, mismatch at hotel check-in etc. Hmm — the dossier's statement is about domestic marker change; the visitor's documents are home-issued. So the open question is how officials treat foreign documents with an X marker or a marker mismatching appearance. Unaddressed — an open question, light weight per rule 13.

No criminalisation. Sexuality law now decriminalised — a positive climate signal (regional outlier in a region where six countries still criminalise). Court's interpretive holding on SOGI in sex discrimination — climate signal of institutional respect.

No documented trans-specific violence (single assault on activist pre-2022, weak). No documented police targeting. No facility restrictions documented. No documented universal-exposure measure.

Thin dossier. Per rule 13/17 (weak signals extrapolate), what structural signals? Decriminalisation via strong court ruling, constitutional SOGI interpretation, official acknowledgement that LGBTQ people aren't persecuted. Absence of antidiscrimination law and LGR = resident gaps, lightest weight. Undocumented areas: border practice, custody, healthcare, restrooms — open questions, light, not exposures.

So this looks like roughly the 0.65–0.70 band: no criminalisation, no documented targeting, some positive institutional signals (court ruling, decriminalisation in a hostile region), but thin on visitor-facing protections and no demonstrated social acceptance documentation, no working remedies documented, no equality tribunal, residual social conservatism in the region, no anti-discrimination statute.

Calibration: 0.65 anchors had either documented enforcement/recourse (Avalet), documented social acceptance (Valess), or uneven remedies. Here there is no documented visitor-facing remedy at all, no documented social acceptance research. 0.75 anchors had documented working remedies plus acceptance. So this sits below 0.75. Is it at 0.65 or lower?

Compared to 0.55 anchors: those had documented recurring visitor-facing harms (service refusals, harassment in hotels, police misconduct at borders). Here we have no documented visitor-facing harm at all — a silent dossier. Rule 3: in a well-documented state silence is a moderately positive signal; in a thin-data state it is not. Is this well documented? The dossier is fairly detailed on legal matters but thin on police practice and visitor experience. It's a small jurisdiction probably with limited documentation. So silence should not be read as strong safety.

Hmm. But there's nothing documented that harms visitors. The only trans-specific negative is absence of LGR (resident gap, lightest weight) and no anti-discrimination statute (resident gap). Plus the note that a trans visitor travelling with a partner classified as same-sex would have no relationship recognition — that's a moderate concern but not really a safety exposure; recognition matters if e.g. hospital visitation, but no criminalisation now.

Also: the constitutional SOGI holding is a documented positive of the institutional kind — counts per rule 3 burden-of-proof symmetry.

I'd put this around 0.65. Let's consider whether lower. Rubric rule 21 band implication: universal-exposure practices or discrimination prevalence at scale without remedy → Elevated. Neither documented. So no basis to drop into Elevated. Absence of criminalisation plus functioning courts (a court struck down a statute against government resistance — real rule of law) and no documented targeting → Reduced Risk band.

Within Reduced (0.60–0.80): no documented acceptance research, no documented visitor-facing remedies, thin-data silence. 0.65 seems right; maybe 0.68. I'll go 0.66.
